title: Oracle complexity of stochastic approximate stationarity
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the worst-case number \(Q(\varepsilon)\) of stochastic first-order oracle calls required to output a point \(X\) with \(\mathbb E\|\nabla f(X)\|_2\leq\varepsilon\) for a possibly nonconvex function with gradient Lipschitz constant at most one, initial objective gap at most one, and an unbiased gradient oracle with variance at most one. The worst case includes arbitrary finite dimension. This selected standard form of the source direction is resolved: \(Q(\varepsilon)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-4})\).

why: This question established the basic information cost of approximate stationarity with stochastic gradients in nonconvex optimization. Its resolution identifies when ordinary stochastic gradient complexity is unavoidable and why additional assumptions on the noise are essential for faster rates. It is retained as a complete historical record rather than an active open challenge.
status_note: Resolved in the explicitly selected bounded-variance stochastic first-order model by the matching upper bound and the Arjevani–Carmon–Duchi–Foster–Srebro–Woodworth lower bound, published in 2023. Model and theorem correspondence checked on 13 September 2026. This is a literature resolution, not a claim of an existing Lean proof.

importance.reason: A fundamental minimax benchmark for stochastic nonconvex optimization, now resolved in the selected standard model; its historical significance is independent of archival status.

sentences: Stochastic optimization receives noisy information about an objective and often aims to find a point with small gradient.
The extracted passage asks for a sharp account of the oracle complexity of reaching such approximate stationarity.
Its surrounding discussion includes nonconvex functions, where global minimization is generally too demanding a target.
The same paper develops nearly matching results for the convex setting, so those resolved cases must be separated from the broader motivation.
The remaining research direction is to identify optimal stochastic information requirements under explicitly stated smoothness, noise, and function-class assumptions.

definitions:
In dimension \(d\geq1\), the unknown objective \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable, \(\inf_x f(x)>-\infty\), \(f(0)-\inf_x f(x)\leq1\), and \(\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_2\leq\|x-y\|_2\) for all \(x,y\). An oracle has a fixed distribution for a random variable \(z\) and a jointly measurable map \(g(x,z)\) satisfying \(\mathbb E_z g(x,z)=
abla f(x)\) and \(\mathbb E_z\|g(x,z)-
abla f(x)\|_2^2\leq1\) at every point. Each call at \(x\) uses a fresh independent \(z\) and returns \((f(x),g(x,z))\), so even the exact function value is available. Calls can be adaptive and can use any points in \(\mathbb R^d\). A randomized algorithm consists of measurable decision maps with a private random seed independent of oracle randomness; local computation and memory are unrestricted. After at most \(T\) calls on every run it outputs a measurable point \(X\), which need not be a previous query. For \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/4\), let \(Q(\varepsilon)\) be the least integer \(T\) such that, for every dimension \(d\), there is an algorithm depending on \(d,\varepsilon\) but not on the unknown objective or oracle, with \(\mathbb E\|
abla f(X)\|_2\leq\varepsilon\) for every admissible pair \((f,g)\). The expectation includes both kinds of randomness. If no such uniform query budget across dimensions exists, set \(Q=\infty\). Algorithms may be nonuniform in dimension; the claimed upper bound also has a uniform implementation. There is no almost-sure bound on the gradient noise, no finite-sum promise and no assumption that the same noise sample gives a smooth function of the query point. A sample cannot be saved and reused for a later query.
answer_criterion: For this historical resolved target, establish in Lean a dimension-independent upper bound and a worst-case lower bound matching within universal constant factors for all sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\). The published resolution supplies the claimed rate, but this record does not claim that its proof has already been formalized in Lean. An upper bound alone, or a lower bound only for algorithms restricted to spans of previous gradients, would not meet the original criterion.

context_blocks.text: Foster and coauthors’ 2019 introduction uses the then-incomplete understanding of nonconvex stochastic stationarity as motivation for a paper whose own main bounds concern convex optimization. The inherited extraction did not specify a single noise model. This review explicitly selects the standard bounded-variance, smooth nonconvex model and records its subsequent resolution.

The global statistical oracle also studied in that convex paper provides an entire sampled function. It is different from the pointwise first-order oracle here. The exact scalar function value returned at a queried point is not that global access.

Ghadimi and Lan’s stochastic first-order analysis gives the required order of upper bound. Arjevani and coauthors prove a matching lower bound for arbitrary randomized methods, including oracles that supply exact function values. Their Theorem 3 and its proof use finite dimensions growing with inverse accuracy, which is permitted by this dimension-free worst case.

The lower-bound paper measures stationarity at a query point. Allowing an arbitrary final output changes the budget by at most one query, because the algorithm can query its selected output before stopping. This leaves the asymptotic rate unchanged.

Under the additional mean-squared smoothness assumption and access allowing evaluations with shared randomness, the same paper obtains a different cubic inverse-accuracy rate. That stronger oracle setting does not contradict the quartic rate above.

Small gradient is a stationarity guarantee, not a guarantee of a local or global minimum. Even a completely specified and historically important question should leave the active open-problem benchmark once its selected target is matched to a published resolution.
